lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record--For the Appellant. 

Shafiq Ahmed, Senior Advocate (Tabarak Hossain, Advocate with him) instructed by AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on-Record---For the Respondent No. 1. 

Respondent Nos. 2-6---Not Represented.
parties:
Ruhul Amin ------ Appellant
vs
Official Liquidator, Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 9-5-1984 passed by the High Court Division in Suit No. 1 of 1981).
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J: This appeal by leave, at the instance of the proforma defendant No. 6, is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-5-1984 of the High Court Division passed in Suit No. 1 of 1981 decreeing the suit upon declaring that the property described in the schedule of the plaint belonged to Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd (in liquidation), the bank, and that the defendants have no right, title or interest in the land in suit, the registered deed of sale No. 5870 dated 29-9-1958 executed by Madhabi Lata Lala in favour of the defendant No. 2, only insofar sale of the suit plot is concerned, is null and void, the bank would be entitled to recover khas possession of the suit property by evicting the defendants and removing structures from the suit property except the defendant No. 4, who shall pay to the bank such sum as may be determined by the Court on an application to be filed by the Officer Liquidator of this bank or the said defendant No. 4 to perfect its title to that portion of the suit property which is in its occupation and the said defendant may recover his said sum from defendant Nos. 1 and 3 and the defendant Nos. 1, 5 and 6 may negotiate with the Official Liquidator of the bank for realisation of possession of those parts of the suit property which are in their possession on payment of such sum as may be agreed upon subject to the approval of the Court upon an application by either the Official Liquidator or the defendant Nos. 1, 5 and 6 to be concluded within 1 year from the date of drawing up of the order of the Court failing which the official Liquidator would be at liberty to execute the instant order of the Court.

2. The respondent No. 1, the Official Liquidator of the bank, filed the above suit seeking declaration that the suit property belongs to the bank and the defendants have no right, title, interest and possession in the same and that if the suit property or part thereof is found to be not in possession of the bank then restore possession of the same in its favour on the averments that Sarada Kripa Lala was the owner of the suit property, that is RS Plot No. 2956 in RS Khatian No. 776 corresponding to CS Plot No. 1748 (Part under CS Khatian No. 41 comprising 8.81 acres of land of Mouza East Nasirabad, Chittagong and he, in the year 1929, as security against loans granted to him by the bank, mortgaged the same with the bank along with his other properties, by way of depositing of title deeds and also delivering the possession of the suit property to the bank; then the bank filed an application for mutation of the suit property along with other properties and the Khashmahal Tahsilder, Sadar, Chittagong by order dated 7-1-36 passed in Judicial Miscellaneous (JM) Case No. 236 of 1936-37 mutated the name of the bank in the suit property; Sarada Kripa Lala having failed to repay the loans, the bank filed mortgage suit and obtaining decree filed Mortgage Execution Case No. 51 of 1952 and therein purchased the suit property along with other mortgaged properties; one Haroon Matin filed Money Suit No. 5 of 1957 against the bank claiming Taka 21,000 as damages stating that he, along with Allah Rakha Bai, took lease of the suit property as well as six other plots from the bank for 99 years and subsequently it transpired that the bank had no title on the properties leased to them and the bank, by misrepresentation, leased the same to them and then on obtaining decree dated 14-2-1959 in the above suit, Haroon Matin filed Money Execution Case No. 25 of 1959 wherein he, in collusion with the  then officials of the bank, managed to auction purchase the suit property as well as other six plots in the name of his father, the defendant No. 2; after the bank was wound up by order dated 18-3-1960, the Official Liquidator of the bank filed Pauper Miscellaneous Case No. 100 of 1960 to set aside the above auction sale of the properties of the bank which, subsequently being transferred to the High Court, Dhaka in terms of section 61 of the Banking Companies Ordinance, 1962, was renumbered as Transferred Suit No. 1 of 1981 and, after hearing, the High Court, Dhaka, by judgment and order dated 22-12-1966, decreed the suit declaring the above leases in favour of Haroon Matin and another as well as the subsequent auction purchase of the suit property in the name of defendant No. 2 in Money Execution Case No. 25 of 1959 as null and void with the observation that the officials of the bank, who were in charge of the litigation, had colluded with Haroon Matin. As against that, Haroon Matin filed Letters Patent Appeal No. 4 of 1967 and a Division Bench of the High Court Dhaka by judgment and order dated 31-3-1977 dismissed the above appeal.

3. Then Haroon Matin filed Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979 and the Appellate Division, after hearing, taking into consideration of the provisions of section 73 of the Banking Companies Act 1962 and the case of Official Receiver vs Das Bank Ltd reported in 27 DLR (AD) 133 by judgment and order dated 25-6-80 upheld the above judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 31-1-1977 with the observation that "there can be no doubt that the leases forming parts of the same transaction by fraud and collusion will fall together being void ab initio"; then during spot verification of the suit property in the year 1980 the Official Liquidator came to know that both the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 claimed title in the suit property and litigations are pending; further in reply to the query made by the Official Liquidator to the defendant No. 1 regarding the basis of his claim, the defendant No. 1 by his letter dated 28-11-80 informed the Official Liquidator that in the year 1907 Apparna Charan, his father, took lease of CS Plot No. 1748 from Sadar Khashmahal, Chittagong and the relevant documents of the above lease have been filed by him in the High Court Division in connection with the aforesaid First Appeal No. 115 of 1965. Further case of the bank was, that the suit property being requisitioned in LA Case No. 62/1942-43 during Second World War was taken over for use of the military but later on was derequisitioned on 12-12-1946, and possession was handed over to the bank on 20-1-1947 and that although the defendant No. 1 in his letter dated 28th November, 1980 claimed title over the suit property tracing back his title from the year 1907 but from the records it will be evident that the suit property was owned by Sarada Kripa Lala as recorded owner till 6th November, 1936 and thereafter the same was owned by the bank and that the defendant No. 1, without serving any notice upon the bank, got the suit property mutated in his name in JM Case No. 230A/11 of 1954-55.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and proforma defendant No. 6 who filed joint affidavit in opposition contending, inter alia, that the suit property actually appertained to original Jote No. 88/88 of Mouza East Nasirabad, which was created in Settlement Case No. 284 of 1907-1908 in favour of Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, and the said jote comprised the lands of CS Plot Nos. 1609, 1736 and 1748 and on 29-11-1912 Aparna Charan, filed an application before the Khashmahal Office for demarcation of the said jote land which was registered as Judicial Miscellaneous Case (JM Case) No. 288 of 1911-12 and order was passed therein on 26-3-1912 for demarcation of the lands settled in favour of Aparna Charan and accordingly, demarcation was made by an Amin of the said office on 26-3-1912 and since the creation of the said jote Aparna Charan had been in exclusive possession of the suit property and he had brick fields therein as well as the adjoining lands and during RS operation major portion of the said Jote No. 88/88 was recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1 as RS Jote No. 81 and by mistake the remaining portion, i.e. the suit property comprising of RS Plot No, 2956 appertaining to RS Khatian No. 776, was wrongly recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala as RS Jote No. 86 though he had no title or possession therein and that the defendant No. 1, after death of his father in the year 1929, had also been in continuous possession thereof over the statutory period of limitation and also used the suit land as a part of his brick field and after coming to know that the bank wrongly entered its name in the RS record in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37, filed an application praying for mutation of his name upon correction of the aforesaid wrong entry in the name of the bank and the said application to the Khashmohal Office, Sadar, Chittagong, was registered as JM Case No. 230A/11 of 1554-55 and then notice was duly served upon the bank and in spite of receiving the notice the bank, having no interest in the suit property, did not contest the said application and then the right, title, interest and possession of the defendant No. 1 being found in Jote No. 86 after proper enquiry, by order dated 30-3-1955 the suit property, along with other properties, were recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1 and as far back as 1959 he sold a part of the suit land measuring 1.20 acres to Pakistan Tobacco Co Ltd, the predecessor in interest of Bangladesh Tobacco Co Ltd, the defendant No. 3, who after enjoying the said property till 1964 disposed of the same in favour of State Bank of Pakistan, the predecessor of Bangladesh Bank, the defendant No. 4, whose name has been duly recorded in the record of rights and who is in possession of the same by paying rents regularly; the defendant No. 5 is in possession of part of the suit property by virtue of his purchase from a subsequent transferee of the defendant No. 1 and the proforma defendant No. 6 is in possession of part of the suit property by virtue of direct purchase from the defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 1 has made similar transfers from the suit property to various other purchasers and they, after constructing pucca buildings on portions of the suit property so purchased are in possession of the same long over the statutory period of limitation openly and adversely and since they were not made parties, the suit is bad for defect of parties and neither Sarada Kripa Lala nor the bank had ever any possession, right, title or interest in the suit property.

5. The defendant No. 2 also contested the suit and filed separate affidavit-in-opposition contending that Sarada Kripa Lala never mortgaged the suit property to the bank the suit property did not become the subject matter of the mortgage suit as well as the execution case and that the suit property was rightly recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala during RS operation wherein his status has been recorded as a sthitiban raiyat and he on 4-3-29, made a will bequeathing the suit jote to Madhabi Lata Lala, his daughter-in-law, who, on 17-12-1940 after obtaining probate in Probate Suit No. 4 of 1939 was in continuous and uninterrupted possession of the same on payment of rent and she, after obtaining per-mission from the concerned authority under section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and also obtaining Income Tax Clearance Certificates, sold the suit jote to the defendant No. 2 by kabala dated 29-9-1958 and thus the defendant No. 2 became the absolute owner in possession of the suit jote and his title has also been perfected by lapse of time and that the defendant No. 1, having fraudulently got his name mutated in RS Jote No. 86 and resisted the mutation of the name of this defendant and also the possession of the defendant No. 2 in the suit jote, he filed Other Class Suit No. 49 of  1959 for declaration of his title in the suit jote and also for recovery of khas possession which being dismissed he preferred First Appeal No. 115 of 1965 before the High Court, Dhaka which is pending.

6. The defendant No. 4, Bangladesh Bank, also filed an affidavit-in-opposition stating that on 11-2-1964 they purchased 1.20 acres of land from the suit property from the defendant No. 3 for valuable consideration and since purchase they had been in possession of the same openly and adversely for more than the statutory period of limitation and they were never aware of any claim of title of Sarada Kripa Lala or of the bank in the suit property and that since the valuation of the suit land has increased by 100 times since 1964, in case it is found that the defendant No. 1 and/or the defendant No. 3 had no valid right, title interest in the suit land, they are entitled to be adequately indemnified.

7. The High Court Division, after hearing, decreed the suit.

8. As regards defect of parties, the High Court Division held hat Order I, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes it clear that misjoinder or non-joinder of parties is not fatal to a suit provided the suit is of such a nature that the rights and interests of the parties before the Court can be effectively disposed of without the presence of parties not joined and that in the present case, the transferees of the defendant No. 1 will stand or fall along with the said defendant No. 1 and so in their absence the right, title and interest of the parties may be effectively disposed of and so the suit will not fail for non-joinder of the parties who purchased lands from the defendant No. 1.

9. As regards the case of the bank that Sarada Kripa Lala, along with other properties, also mortgaged the suit property to the bank and the bank purchased the suit property in auction held in Mortgage Execution Case No. 51 of 1952 and they also acquired title by adverse possession, the High Court Division observed:

"There is absolutely no documentary evidence in support of the above contentions On the contrary, by way of furnishing negative evidence, DW 8 Sarat Kumar Kanungoe has proved Exhibit 0, the certified copy of the Power of Attorney No. 686 dated 24-10-1932, which shows that Sarada Kripa Lala nominated and constituted the Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd, to take charge of and manage some of his proper-ties. The schedule of properties does not contain the suit plot. This schedule has been assailed by Dr M Zahir, learned Advocate for the plaintiff, as a forged one. It is very much a part of the certified copy. Besides, if it is the case of the plaintiff that the schedule contains the suit plot or that the suit plot is covered by another Power of Attorney it is open to the plaintiff to produce the certified copies thereof. It did not do so."

"DW 11 deposing on behalf of the defendant No. 2 has proved Exhibits 11 and JJ, both certified copies of sale certificates in Mortgage Execution Case Nos. 51 of 1952 and 63 of 1944 respectively. The properties of Sarada Kripa Lala were auction purchased by Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd, in these two Mortgage Execution Cases. Exhibits 11 and JJ do not show that the suit plot was included in the said auction purchases. If the suit Plot No. 2956 was auction purchased in another mortgage execution case, it was perfectly open to the plaintiff to produce the certified copy of the relevant sale certificate. It did not do so. I therefore, hold that suit plot No. 2956 was not mortgaged by Sarada Kripa Lala to the Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd, in 1929 or at any time. It was not the subject matter of any mortgage suit or mortgage decree. It was never auction purchased by the Bank."

"The learned Advocate for the defendants have not opposed Dr M Zahir's plea to consider the case of adverse possession. They have of course argued that adverse possession has not been established, which I shall duly take note of. In those circumstances I do not think that the defendants will be prejudiced at all if the plea of adverse possession, raised by the plaintiff is considered in the light of the entire evidence on record, though not specifically raised in the plaint. In support of his case of adverse possession Dr M Zahir has relied upon Exhibit 4, certified copy of the proceedings of JM Case No. 236-37, Exhibit 1, the certified copy of the corrected RS Record of rights of the suit khatian and Exhibit 5 the copy of the proceedings of LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43."

"With regard to the oral evidence on possession, PW 1 Md Shahjahan has stated that he joined Bangladesh Bank only in April, 1981. He has deposed with reference to the papers and documents available to him. He has no personal knowledge about possession. Therefore the plaintiff's case on adverse possession in based on documentary evidence only."

"Thus it is clear that the Bank itself was under a mistaken belief that it was a mortgagee in possession in respect of RS Jote No. 86. It's application in respect of RS Jote No. 86 for mutation was founded on that behalf. The Khashmohal also granted the Bank's prayer in the way it wanted. But in actual fact there was no mortgage of RS Jote No. 86. The application for mutation as a mortgagee in possession was a mistaken application. The actual mutation was a mortgagee in possession does not also reflect the correct position. The correct possession is that the Bank entered into possession of RS Jote No. 86 mistakenly as a mortgagee."

Exhibit 5 is the next document relied upon my Dr M Zahir. It is the certified copy of the proceeding of LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43. It appears from the compensation schedule that RS Plot No. 2956 was requisitioned by the land Acquisition Department during the World War II in the said LA Case and occupied by the Military authorities on 30-11-1942. It also shows that the Mahluxmi Bank Ltd, was entered in the compensation schedule as the owner in possession of RS Plot No. 2956  ..... That finding recording the contemporaneous possession of the Bank remains a strong piece of evidence in favour of the plaintiff unchallenged subsequently by Sarada Kripa Lala. He or any one also claiming through him did not file any suit challenging the recording of RS Plot No. 2956 in favour of the Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd, as far back as in 1936. Although it is quite probable that the bank took possession of the suit plot on 24-10-1932 when it took possession of the other mortgaged properties of Sarada Kripa Lala, I shall not go by probabilities, but evidence. I shall take Exhibit 4 as the evidence of contemporaneous maters, not as an evidence of matters past. I have also taken note of the fact that Exhibit 4 remains unchallenged by the defendants. It has also not been assailed on any ground whatsoever."

10. The High Court Division also found that the defendant No. 1 claimed that most of the land settled in favour of Aparna Charan, his father, were in RS Jote No. 81 but some part thereof was recorded wrongly in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in RS Jote No. 86 and after coming to know about the same from the defendant No. 2 for the first time in the year 1954 he filed JM Case No. 230 of 1954-55 but the above claim is not correct as there is no corroboration from any witness in this regard and the fact that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the full CS Plot No. 1748 and took settlement of a part of it is evident from Exhibit F, i.e. the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 284 of 1907-08 for settlement, Exhibit G i.e. the list of tenants, Exhibit H i.e. the kabuliyat executed by Aparna Charan, Exhibit S(6) i.e. sale deed dated 26-7-1939 executed on behalf of the defendant No. 1 in favour of Jibendra Lal Dutta and Exhibit S(7) i.e. the sale deed dated 5-8-1942 executed by Jibendra Lal Dutta in favour of the defendant No. 1 which will show that the Aparna Charan entered into possession of the full CS Plot No. 1748 after demarcation of boundaries in the year 1912 and then, as will be evident from Exhibits A-A4, he retreated to the settled portion of CS Plot No. 1748 at the time of RS operation and was not in possession of RS Plot No. 2956 at the time of preparation of RS records as is evidenced by Exhibit E(1), the RS Khatian No. 776, and that is why RS Plot No. 2956 was recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala who actually possessed the suit property at the time of RS operation and the defendant No. 1 has failed to rebut the presumption of RS records by any documentary or unimpeachable oral evidence and as has been held in the case of Alimuddin Munshi vs Mainuddin Talukder, 14 DLR 725, merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of rights, the presumption under the entry is not rebutted and there must be further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect and the defendant No. 1 having failed to produce any documentary evidence or any convincing evidence to show that and further the non-payment of rent by the defendant No. 1 for RS Plot No. 2956 from 1930 to 1955 was not an inadvertence as has been urged and, on the other hand, such non payment supports that the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor had no interest in the suit property and that is why they did not pay rent for the suit property after the RS operation and further from 1930 to 1955 the defendant No. 1 and his predecessor were quite happy and content with the recording of the land settled in favour of Aparna Charan in RS Jote No. 81 and Aparna Charan paid rent for that jote in the justified belief that all the settled lands of Aparna Charan were included in it and several transactions were made in respect of the lands of Jote No. 81 with the clear understanding and belief that those dealings were in respect of the entire settled lands of Aparna Charan and the defendant No. 1 took certified copies of his father's settlement papers, Exhibits F-H in the year 1954 and he failed to show any other certified copy taken before 1954 and further, taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank in the year 1954, the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property in the year 1955 and showing interpolated Exhibits F-H obtained mutation of the suit property in his own name and started the brick field during Pakistan period as unwittingly given out by DWs 1 and 2 and then he paid rent for RS Jote No. 86 from 1955 onwards and sold 1.20 acres of the suit land to Pakistan Tobacco Co Ltd in the year 1956 and in the year 1965 he stopped manufacturing bricks and on dividing the suit property into many plots started selling those to willing purchasers till an order of status quo was passed by the High Court Division and while the bank has been able to prove that it had possession of the suit land from 1934-55 by documentary evidence and, on the other hand, the defendant No. 1 has no documentary evidence and/or any reliable oral evidence in support of his title and possession of the suit land from 1930-55 and as has been held in the case of Keshav Raghunath Deshpande vs Govind Chimnaji Deshpande, AIR 1928 Bom 287 the fact that a stranger in the present case, the bank takes possession of a property under a mistake common to all does not make his possession any less adverse and it has also been held in a number of cases, namely, Govinda vs Mallayya, 311 C 678, Kunwar Sen vs Darbarilal ILR 38 All 411, Ram Piari vs Budhsen ILR 43 All 164, Priya Sakhi vs Manbodh Bibi, ILR 44 Cal 425, that a mortgagee, who does not enter possession in his character as mortgagee, may by 12 years' adverse possession, acquire a good title against a mortgagor and in a number of cases, namely, Zaibunnessa vs Parichit, 23, IC 611, Mula Singh vs Budh Singh, 25 IC 616, and Bhari vs Abbayanath, 41, IC 862, it has also been held that a mortgagee may by 12 years' adverse possession, acquire a good title to other land of the mortgagor which had not been validly mortgaged to him and that in the present case adverse possession of the bank against Sarada Kripa Lala and his successor started from the date of mutation on 7-11-36 and the bank continued in possession and its possession stood reconfirmed during the requisition and derequisition proceedings in 1942 and 1946-47 and that in the year 1942 the defendant No. 1 re-purchased RS Jote No. 81 being fully satisfied that this was the entire settled land of his father and further, the defendant No. 1 or Sarada Kripa Lala was no where in the picture during the requisition and de-requisition proceedings and therefore taking the date of the possession of the bank to be 7-11-36, the bank acquired good title to the suit land by adverse possession and so Madhabi Lata Lala had no saleable interest in the suit land on 29-9-58 and though Mr Mahmudul Islam, relying on the case of Sarat Chandra Maiti vs Bibhaboti Debi AIR 1921 Calcutta 584, submitted that when a property is requisitioned it passes into legal custody and during the continuance of requisition such custody is for the benefit of the true owner but the above cited case is a case of attachment under section 146, CrPC and there is nothing to show that such an order of attachment under section 146, CrPC is applicable in the case of mortgage.

11. Being aggrieved by the above judgment and decree of the High Court Division, the proforma defendant No. 6, who is a successor of the defendant No. 1, preferred Appeal No. 12 of 1984 before a Division Bench of the High Court Division under section 72 of the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962 and by judgment and order dated 20-4-2000 the High Court Division dismissed the appeal holding that the above appeal is not maintainable as the provisions of Letter Patent Appeal was abolished by the Law Reforms Ordinance 1978 and then leave was sought.

12. Leave was granted on the submissions that the defendant No. 1 transferred the major portion of the suit property to others long before the institution of the instant suit and those transferees having not been impleaded inspite of objection taken and, as such, the suit is bad for defect of parties and the High Court Division, upon an erroneous view, held that since those transferees will stand or fall with the defendant No. 1; the learned Single Judge having found that the bank was not a mortgagee in respect of the suit property and that the suit land was wrongly mutated in the name of the bank as a mortgagee in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 and that "the actual mutation as a mortgagee in possession does not also reflect the correct position" and there having been absolutely no oral evidence of possession by the bank, committed grave error of law in finding title of the bank by adverse possession on the basis of the order of mutation of the suit property in the above JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 specially when in their pleading the bank did not plead that they acquired title adverse possession; there having been no evidence whatsoever of the bank's entering into possession of the suit property the learned Single Judge was manifestly wrong in holding that the correct position was that the bank entered into possession of the suit property mistakenly as a mortgagee and such a finding is solely based on surmise and conjecture; even if it is assumed for argument's sake, without however conceding that the plaintiff bank entered into possession of the suit property in the year 1936, the learned Single Judge failed to notice that the bank claiming to have entered in possession as a mortgagee and having neither pleaded nor adduced evidence to show from when the plaintiff asserted absolute title to the disputed land;, the defendant No. 1 having examined a number of person to prove his possession in the suit property and there having been no evidence adduced by either the bank or defendant No. 2 in support of this adverse possession, the learned Single Judge ought to have held that the defendant No. 1, all through, had been in possession of the suit property; the learned Single Judge misread Exhibit 5, the certified copy of the proceedings of Land Acquisition of LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43 to find possession of the bank, inasmuch as Exhibit 5 neither shows that possession of the suit property was taken from the bank nor shows that the said property was redelivered to the bank upon de-requisition and even if it is assumed for argument's sake without however conceding that the bank was in possession of the suit property prior to 30-11-1942, when the government took possession of the same the bank being a trespasser could not tack the period between 30-11-1942 and 38-1-1947 for acquisition of title by adverse possession, inasmuch as the government having taken over possession of the suit property under the law, the possession of the bank was snapped and fresh period of limitation would start to run from the time the suit property was derequisitioned and vacated by the government, Exhibit A series, i.e. the proceedings of Boundary Demarcation Miscellaneous Case No. 288 of 1911-12 and Exhibit N, the rent receipt taken together with other documents clearly establish that Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, took settlement of the entire CS Plot No. 1748 of which the suit property was a part and he possessed the same until his death in the year 1929, before RS operation, and the learned Single Judge upon untenable ground disbelieved the case of the defendant No. 1 claiming title to the entire CS Plot No. 1748 including the suit property and failed to consider that the documents produced by him and particularly, the records of Exhibit A series and the map prepared by the Amin therein, clearly established the claim of the defendant No. 1 and also shows that the entry of the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in the RS record of rights is completely without basis, the learned Single Judge on the basis of Report of JM Case No. 230A/ 11 of 1954-55, having found Exhibit R(1), that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property in 1955 and the defendant No. 1 adduced oral evidence in support of his possession, whereas there having been no evidence as to how the bank came into possession of the suit property, ought to have held that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property ever since it was derequisitioned in 1947; the present proceeding being for recovery of possession the burden of proof was on the bank, the plaintiff to, prove its possession and the bank having failed to adduce any evidence in this regard the defendant No. 1 was not required to adduce any evidence of possession and, in this state of affairs, when the preponderance of evidence regarding possession was heavily in favour of the defendant No. 1, the learned Single Judge ignoring the preponderance of evidence wrongly found that the defendant No. 1 was not in possession of the suit property prior to 1955; the finding of the learned Single Judge that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the entire CS plot No. 1748 and that Sarada Kripa Lala was in possession of the suit property at the time of RS operation and that the defendant No. 1 failed to rebut the presumption of the RS record of rights and the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank are all contrary to the evidence on record and are the result of surmise and conjecture.

13. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for the appellant, in his submission reiterated the grounds as stated above and also submitted that the High Court Division fell in error in relying on Exhibit AA, alleged traced copy of the CS map, to hold that CS Plot No. 1748 was sub-divided before RS Operation, inasmuch as Exhibit AA is only a traced copy and there is no evidence on record to show that any competent authority passed any order to treat Exhibit AA as an original CS map, and specially when it does not satisfy the requirement of section 83 of the Evidence Act and further, the High Court Division also fell in error in not taking into consideration the judgment and order passed in Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979 as being not inter parties without considering that the said judgment and order, though not inter parties, was admissible under section 13 of the Evidence Act to prove the fact that the relevant original CS map along with a traced copy was filed in that suit and no division or Bata-dags were shown in the original CS map while such division was shown in the traced copy.

14. Mr Shafiq Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1, submitted that although plea of adverse possession was not raised in the pleading but issue No. 6 specifically related to adverse possession and the defendants led evidence in this regard and before the witnesses were examined the learned Advocate for the bank made oral submission that the bank would claim title by adverse as well and the learned Advocate for the defendants did not oppose the above submission and argued that the defendant No. 1 failed to establish his adverse possession on the suit property by adequate evidence and, in view of the above, the High Court Division was competent in considering the case of adverse possession in the light of entire evidence on record and on consideration of evidence on record, particularly order sheet of JM Case No. 234 of 1936-37, Exhibit 4 the High Court Division rightly came to the finding that the bank entered into possession of the suit property in the year 1936 on the basis of order dated 7-11-36 passed in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 and continued its possession till 1955 and the Government took over possession of the suit property on 30-11-1942 in LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43 and then the same was returned to the bank on 8-1-47 and the period in which the suit land was under the occupation of the military has been rightly construed by the learned Single Judge to be the possession of the bank and further Exhibit 8, the judgment passed In Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979, was rightly considered by the High Court Division in deciding the suit and the defendant No. 1, as DW 8, in his evidence clearly stated that his father Apama Charan took settlement of some land including the suit land in the year 1907 and the quantum of land was 36 acres but Exhibit A series showed that the total area of land alleged to have been settled was 64.32 acres and, as such, the above discrepancy falsify the above claim of the defendant No. 1 of taking settlement of 36 acres of land by Aparna Charan and further DW 8 in his deposition clearly stated that he has no documentary evidence regarding taking possession of the suit property prior to 1955 except his oral evidence and the other witnesses in support of possession of the defendant No. 1 having contradicted each other in material points, the possession of the defendant No. 1, since taking alleged settlement by his father in 1907, remained not proved and the defendant No. 1 also admitted that neither his father nor himself mutated their name before 1955 and, as such, the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in decreeing the suit.

15. We have perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and also other papers on record.

<u>16. Regarding non joinder of the parties who purchased part of the suit property, in the case of Jahan Ara Begum vs AL Md Shamsul Hoque 27 DLR (AD) 129, which is in connection with a suit for specific performance of contract, this Division while interpreting Order I, rule 9 and 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, held, that when effective remedy cannot be given without adding such a party who has not been joined then only the suit will be bad for defect of parties. So we are of the view that the High Court Division, on this point, correctly held that the purchasers of the part of the suit property being the transferees of the defendant No. 1, will stand or fall along with the defendant No. 1 and so in their absence the right, title and interest of the parties may be effectively disposed off.</u>

17. Regarding the point as to the power of the Court to decree the suit on the basis of claim of adverse possession of the plaintiff even in the absence of plea of adverse possession in the pleading, the High Court Division relying on 3 ILR, 4 ILR, 14 ILR as referred earlier, held that even in the absence of a case of adverse possession in the pleading the suit can be decreed on the basis of adverse possession of the plaintiff in the suit property.

18. As it appears in 3 ILR it has been held that where a plaintiff seeks to recover possession of property from which he has been dispossessed and bases his claim on the ground of purchase and also upon the ground of a twelve years' possessory title, he is entitled to succeed if he proves his possession, even if he fails to prove his purchase. In the above case, the possession of the plaintiff in the case land has been proved not only by the evidence of the plaintiff but also by the admission of the defendant.

19. In 4 ILR it was also similarly held that where a person claims possession of property under a specific title, coupled with an allegation that he has been in possession of that property for more than twelve years under that title, he is entitled to a decree on the strength of his twelve years' possession, even though he failed to make out his specific title. In the above cases the plaintiff proved his long possession over 12 years beyond any doubt.

20. In 14 ILR the plaintiff sued to recover possession of certain land, alleging that it was lakhiraj land, which he had purchased from a third party and the Court of first instance having found that he had not proved the title he alleged but proved twelve years' possession decreed the suit. On appeal, the lower appellate Court having found that though 12 years adverse possession had been proved but since acquisition of title by adverse possession was not alleged in the plaint and no issue was raised as to it, the plaintiff was not entitled to succeed. But on appeal the High Court held that as the suit was one for possession and the defendant had express notice in the lower appellate Court that the plaintiff relied on the title of adverse possession, and as the defendant took no objection on the ground that he should be allowed an opportunity to call evidence to rebut it, and as he had consequently not been prejudiced by the course adopted by the lower Appellate Court, the decree of trial Court should be confirmed.

21. As it appears following the decision of 14 ILR Dr Zahir, who appeared in the High Court Division for the bank, before the witnesses were examined, made oral submission that the bank would claim title by adverse possession as well and the learned Advocate for the defendants having not opposed the above plea, the learned Single Judge was of the opinion that the defendants will not be prejudiced at all if the plea of adverse possession raised by the bank is considered in the light of the entire evidence on record, though not specifically raised in the pleading.

22. In the instant case in their pleading the bank did not raise the plea of their acquiring title by adverse possession and so no issue was framed regarding acquiring of title of the bank in the suit land by their adverse possession. However, since the defendant No. 1 asserted that they acquired title also by adverse possession, issue No. 6 was framed regarding the acquiring of title by the defendant No. 1 on the basis of adverse possession.

From the case cited by Mr Islam mentioned herein below, it will appear that the decisions reported in 3 ILR, 4 ILR and 14 ILR do no longer depict the correct proposition of law.

23. In the case of Misir Ali vs Abdul Rashid, 5 DLR 279, referred to by Mr Islam, the plaintiff asserted title by way of adverse possession and it was held that the plaintiff having never set up such a case of adverse possession in the plaint cannot succeed in the suit on the ground that he acquired title by adverse possession as the facts make it absolutely clear that the case is governed by Article 142 of Limitation Act and accordingly, the plaintiff had to establish two things affirmatively, that is he had title and secondly, that he was in possession within twelve years before institution of the suit and even if his possession is made out, he cannot succeed if the title lies with the defendant. So, in the instant case even if the bank proves possession over period of 12 years, they will not succeed if the title remained with the defendant No. 1.

24. In the case of Niropoma Ritchel vs Md Abdul Jalil Mea 41 DLR 467, referred to by Mr Islam the distinction between lawful possession and claiming title by adverse possession was illustrated holding that the most essential elements of adverse possession is that the purchaser of a property by a person having no right to possess the property, such possession must be adverse to the true owner and the question of adverse possession in a case is to be determined on the basis of specific averment made in the plaint and that in a suit for declaration of title on the basis of adverse possession material consideration is the starting point of limitation and alternative title on the basis of adverse possession not having been pleaded and proved, decreeing of the suit by the trial Court without reference to the plaint and evidence on record is illegal and further no issue being framed on the vital question of adverse possession decree is also illegal. In the aforesaid case there was no assertion either in the plaint or in the deposition regarding adverse possession and no issue was also framed regarding acquiring of title by the plaintiff on the basis of adverse possession.

25. In the case of Mahaprabhu Ram vs Gopal Ram 42 DLR (AD) 154 referred to by Mr Islam the case of the appellants was one of acquisition of title by settlement which was not proved on trial and the trial Court conferred title on him on a gratuitous finding of adverse possession, unwarranted by pleading. The High Court Division held that the gratuitous conferment of title was uncalled for in a suit for partition and that of the precise title to which the plaintiff lays his claim is not supported by evidence on record, the Court cannot find out another source of title for him, by way of gratuitous relief.

26. In the case of Gouri Das vs ABM Hasan Kabir 7 BLC (AD) 140 referred to by Mr Islam, argument of adverse possession was advanced submitting that in the terms of section 7(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 a tenant must show that he had been holding the property in question for a period of not less than 12 years without any lease and this Division held that mere suggestion of uninterrupted possession for 12 years or that the plaintiff had acquired an absolute title is not enough and to claim adverse possession it must be specifically pleaded in the plaint and hostile title must be asserted and the adverse possession must be adequate in continuity and furthermore, evidence must be adduced to show when possession became adverse so that the starting point of limitation against the party affected can be found and in the instant appeal, there was no attempt to prove since when the adverse possession has started and there is no evidence when possession became adverse and that long possession is not necessarily adverse possession.

27. In the case of SM Karim vs Bibi Sakina, AIR 1964 SC 1254 it was held that alternative claim by adverse possession must be clearly made and proved and adverse possession must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and extent and a plea is required at the least to show when possession becomes adverse so that the starting point of limitation against the party affected can be found. A mere suggestion in the relief clause that there was an uninterrupted possession for "several 12 years" or that the plaintiff had acquired "an absolute title" was not enough to raise such a plea. Long possession and the prayer clause is not a substitute for a plea.

28. In the case of Mahesh Chand Sharma vs Raj Kumari Sharma AIR 1969 SC 869 it has been held that a person pleading adverse possession has no equities in his favour. Since he is trying to defeat the rights of the true owner, it is for him to clearly plead and establish all the facts necessary to establish his adverse possession. For all the above reasons, the plea of limitation put forward by the appellant or by defendants Nos. 2 to 5 as the case may be is rejected. It was held that a person pleading adverse possession has no equity in his favour and since he trying to defeat the right of the true owner it is for the plaintiff to clearly plead to establish all the facts necessary to establish his adverse possession.

29. As it appears, the High Court Division relying on the case of Govinda vs Mallayya, 31 IC 678, Kunwar Sen vs Darbarilal ILR 38 Allalabad 411, Ram Piari vs Budhsen ILR 43 Allahabad 164 and Priya Sakhi vs Manboodh Bibi, ILR 44 Calcutta 425, further held that a mortgagee, who does not enter possession in his character as mortgagee, may by 12 years' adverse possession, acquire a good title against a mortgagor. The High Court Division relying on the case of Mula Singh vs Budh Singh 25 Indian Cases (1915) 616, Bihari vs Adya, 41 Indian Cases 612 further held that a mortgagee, may, by 12 years of adverse possession acquire good title to the other properties of the mortgagor which had not been mortgaged to him.

30. In 31 IC 678 the plaintiff prayed for redemption of a mortgage and for accounts from the defendant, the mortgagee in possession, and the defendants set up an oral sale by the mortgagor in discharge of the mortgage debt and also adverse possession for more than the statutory period. The plaintiff's suit having been dismissed, he appealed on the grounds that the plea of oral sale was res judicata by reason of the decision in a previous suit and that oral evidence of the alleged sale was inadmissible. It was held that the defendant's possession had been all along adverse as against the mortgagee and that they had acquired a title by prescription. So, in this case the case of adverse possession of a defendant against a mortgagee was decided.

31. In 38 ILR it was held that a person could not acquire a title by adverse possession to land which was the subject of a usufructuary mortgage and therefore in the possession of the mortgagees, merely because he had managed to get his name recorded in the village papers for a series of years in respect of the mortgage property and it must be borne in mind that the equity of redemption where the possession remains with the mortgagor is quite different from the equity of redemption where the possession is with the mortgagee and there can be no doubt that an equitable estate, as distinguished from a legal estate, can be barred by time but it seems to us impossible that any person can be in possession of the right to redeem a mortgage where, under the terms of the mortgage, the mortgagee is entitled to the actual possession, and is in fact in possession thereunder.

32. In 43 ILR a mortgagee in possession professing himself to be the full owner and not merely a mortgagee, mortgaged the property to a third party, whose heirs having brought a suit on their mortgage and obtained a decree, put up the property for sale and purchased it themselves. Subsequently they, by private contract, sold the property which they had purchased. The representatives of the original mortgagors then sued for redemption. In was held that neither article 134 nor article 148 of the first schedule to the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, applied to the suit but article 144 is applicable and the suit was barred as the ultimate purchasers, the defendants, were entitled to add to the period of their possession the period of possession of the auction purchasers, their predecessors.

33. In 44 ILR it was held that adverse possession against the mortgagor is not per se adverse against the mortgagee in the case of a simple mortgage and per Sandersos CJ "Adverse possession affects the interest which the person, who was entitled to immediate possession, had at that time" and per Mookerjee  J. "Section 28 of the Limitation Act clearly contemplates that the person, whose right is extinguished by lapse of time is a person entitled to institute a suit for possession of the property."

34. In 25 India Cases question arose as to the effect of encroachment by the mortgagee on other land of mortgagor and also the effect of his being recorded in settlement paper as mortgagee of encroached land and it was held, that where a mortgagee encroaches upon his mortgagor's land not mortgaged to him, he holds it adversely to the mortgagor from the date of encroachment, although in the Settlement papers the encroached area is also shown as mortgaged property.

35. In 41 Indian Cases it was held that where a person has been in possession of land in the open assertion of a definite and specific right as mortgagee, it is not open to the owner of the land to question his right after the expiry of more than twelve years from the date when such open assertion was made within his knowledge or within the knowledge of his predecessor-in-title.

36. As it appears, the facts of the above case are not similar to the facts of the instant case. Further in the case of P Lakshmi Reddy vs L Lakshmi Reddy, AIR 1957 SC 314 referred by Mr Islam, it was held that a mere suggestion in the relief clause that there was an uninterrupted possession for "several 12 years" or that the plaintiff had acquired "an absolute title" was not enough to raise such a plea and long possession and the prayer clause is not a substitute for a plea.

37. As it appears the High Court Division found that the suit property was not mortgaged in favour of the bank and the bank also did not purchase the suit property held in auction held in Mortgage Execution Case No. 51 of 1952 and as is evident from Exhibit 00 the bank got possession of the suit property from Sarada Kripa Lala for its management and control. So, the possession of the bank, in such circumstances, may not be similar to that of a receiver but near to that. In the case of Sarat Chandra Maiti vs Bibhabati Debi AIR 1921 Calcutta 584 cited by Mr Islam it was held that when a property is attached under section 146, it passes into legal custody, and during the continuance of the attachment, such custody is for the benefit of the true owner. If the true owner was, in fact, in possession when the attachment was effected, his possession in the eye of the law is not interrupted. If, on the other hand, the wrongdoer was in possession at the time when the attachment took place, the effect of the attachment is to interrupt his possession, and from the moment of attachment, the possession of the rightful owner revived in the eye of the law but the High Court Division held that since the above decision is in respect of proceeding under section 146, CrPC, the same is not applicable in the present case.

38. The High Court Division also relying on the principle being that possession though commenced under a mortgage yet continued under a different capacity starts adverse possession as held in Pandian Pillal vs Vellalyappi, 42 IC 438 decreed the suit but also held that though in the above case the mortgage deed provided that the mortgagee should enjoy the mortgaged properties for a certain period and that after that date, if the principal is not paid, the property should become absolutely his but the above provision does not convert the mortgage into an usufructuary one, nor does the sale become absolute after the stipulated period and such a provision is a clog on the equity of redemption and must be relieved against and the above provision has been introduced not as a term of the mortgage but only as limiting the term of enjoyment in lieu of interest.

39. The High Court Division relying on the case of Keshav Raghunath Deshpande vs Govind Chimanaji Deshpande AIR 1928 Bombay 287 wherein it was held that the fact that a stranger takes possession of a property under a mistake common to all does not make his possession any the less adverse but adverse possession must be adequate in continuity, publicity and extent so as to show that it is possession adverse to the competitor held that the bank acquired title in the suit property on the basis of its adverse possession therein but failed to consider that in the above case, Chimanaji and Raghunath, being the sons of Narayan, all along remained in possession of the property with the tacit acquiescence and consent of each other and it is, therefore, difficult to hold that there could, under such circumstances, be any adverse possession on the part of Chimanaji as against Raghunath with regard to the undivided moiety of the property.

40. As it appears in the present case the bank with the consent of Sarada Kripa Lala went into possession of the suit property for its management and control of the same and the said position continued.

41. In ILR 13 Madras 467 referred to by Mr Islam the possession of a limited right, that is interest of an mortgagee, came up for consideration wherein the plaintiff Poruppu was a tenant under the Zaminder and he raised the plea that he acquired title by adverse possession and it was held that after twelve years of adverse possession the tenant cannot claim title and Zaminder can claim rent from him.

42. In the case of Hemanta Kumari Debi vs Midnapore Zemindary Co Ltd AIR 1942 (Calcutta) 233 referred by Mr Islam it was held that when the defendant in possession sets up a title only to a limited interest which even if completed would not extinguish the title of the plaintiff and it is for the defendant to establish his title in order to defeat the claim of the plaintiff and the extent of the title acquired by adverse possession depends on the extent of the claim or right under which possession is obtained and kept and if the claim is restricted to a limited interest in the property, e.g. tenancy right in the property, possession is adverse to the extent of that limited interest only and there can be no question of absolute title by adverse possession when only a limited interest has been asserted. In the present case, the bank mutated its name in the suit property that is in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 as a mortgagee, that is, on the basis of limited interest and since the learned Single Judge held that the bank was not a mortgagee and also did not purchase the suit property in auction the bank as is evident from Exhibit 00 held the suit property for its control and management, which means with the consent of Sarada Kripa Lala.

43. In the case of V Ry Hari Sahib vs Ry Sivaji Raja Sahib, AIR 1927 Madras 61 referred by Mr Islam, it was argued for the appellants that the possession of the receiver must be added to their previous adverse possession and that thereby their title by prescription was perfected, but it was held that the possession of a receiver appointed by Court is possession of the person who is found to be the true owner and consequently the possession of the receiver must have been on his behalf and it would be impossible to hold otherwise for, if it were held, that the receiver holds possession on behalf of a trespasser and not on behalf of the true owner, such possession being under orders of Court abetting a trespass and that can certainly never be done and as the possession of the defendants was interrupted, they have not acquired title by prescription and the present suits are not barred by limitation.

44. In the present case even if it is assumed for argument's sake that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property since 1936 adversely, in view of the requisition of the suit property and taking over possession of the same by the government on 30-11-1942 which remained with them till 1947, the possession of the bank was snapped as even if the bank is found to be in possession of the suit property in the year 1942, it was not in a position to file suit against the government for possession. So there was no legal basis for the High Court Division to hold that the bank was also in possession of the suit property from 13-11-1942 to 8-1-1947 and continued the possession till 1955.

<u>45. Further, Exhibit A series, i.e. the proceedings of Boundary Demarcation Miscellaneous Case No. 288 of 1911-12 and Exhibit N, the rent receipt, taken together with other documents established that Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, took settlement of the entire CS Plot No. 1748 of which the suit property was a part and he possessed the same until his death in the year 1929, before RS operation and the learned Single Judge upon untenable ground disbelieved the case of the defendant No. 1 claiming title to the entire CS Plot No. 1748 including the suit property. The learned Single Judge also failed to consider that the documents produced by the defendant No. 1, particularly the records of Exhibit A series and the map prepared by the Amin therein, clearly established the claim of the defendant No. 1 in the suit property and also show that the entry of the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in the RS record of rights is completely without basis. The learned Single Judge on the basis of Report of JM Case No. 230A/ 11 of 1954-55, having found Exhibit R(1), that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property in the year 1955 and the defendant No. 1 adduced oral evidence in support of his possession whereas there having been no evidence as to how the bank came into possession of the suit property, ought to have held that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property ever since it was derequisitioned on 8-1-1947 and the present proceeding being for recovery of possession the burden of proof was on the bank, the plaintiff, to prove its possession and the bank having failed to adduce any evidence in this regard the defendant No. 1 was not required to adduce any evidence of possession and in this state of affairs, when the preponderance of evidence regarding possession was heavily in favour of the defendant No. 1, the learned Single Judge ignoring the preponderance of evidence, wrongly found that the defendant No. 1 was not in possession of the suit property prior to 1955. Further, the finding of the learned Single Judge that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the entire CS plot No. 1748 and that Sarada Kripa Lala was in possession of the suit property at the time of RS operation and that the defendant No. 1 failed to rebut the presumption of the RS record of rights and the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank are all contrary to the evidence on record and are the result of surmise and conjecture. It also appears that the learned Single Judge fell in error in relying on Exhibit AA, alleged traced copy of the CS map, to hold that CS Plot No. 1748 was subdivided before RS Operation, inasmuch as Exhibit AA is only a traced copy and there is no evidence on record to show that any competent authority passed any order to treat Exhibit AA as an original CS map and specially when it does not satisfy the requirement of section 83 of the Evidence Act and further, the High Court Division also fell in error in not taking into consideration the judgment and order passed in Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979 as being not inter parties without considering that the said judgment and order, though not inter parties, was admissible under section 13 of the Evidence Act to prove the fact that the relevant original CS map along with a traced copy was filed in that suit and no division or Bata-dags were shown in the original CS map while such division was shown in the traced copy.</u>

<u>Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division cannot be sustained. The appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and the judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside.</u>

End.
